newsitem.title: USA: Ford to push 1997 costs below 1996 levels.
newsitem.headline: Ford to push 1997 costs below 1996 levels.

text.p: Ford Motor Co Chief Financial Officer John Devine said the automaker plans to perform the unprecedented feat of cutting 1997 costs below 1996 levels, but he acknowledged that some cost reduction moves could lead to charges against earnings.

"The major improvement we're going to have in 1997 is our cost structure," Devine told reporters at a news briefing. "And for the first time in our history, if we're successful, our costs in 1997 will be below what they wound up in 1996. That will be the first time ever, as far back as we can tell."

Devine said the largest focus of Ford's cost cutting efforts is material costs, both in Ford's own parts operations and outside suppliers. He declined to offer specific targets, but said Ford's goals are broader than past efforts.
"We're working to focus on total costs -- total cost by vehicles, total cost by area," he said.
"So obviously, if we don't get it in one area, we're going to get it in another area."
Devine said Ford is working on a number of cost reduction efforts in Europe, where its fourth quarter loss swelled to $88 million from $48 million a year earlier.
Asked if some of Ford's initiatives will result in charges against earnings in 1997, Devine said: "There could be. There's nothing on our plate right now, but you never say never."
Devine declined to discuss further Ford's plans to eliminate jobs at its Halewood plant near Liverpool, England, other than to say: "It's a tough situation for all of us."
He reiterated Ford's earlier statements that it is aiming for breakeven performance in Europe in 1997, but said Ford's losses in South America were expected to continue.

Ford lost $642 million in South America, up from $94 million in 1995, because it has had to rebuild its operations in Brazil and Argentina since the dissolution of Ford's Autolatina joint venture with Volkswagen AG in 1995.

Devine also said credit losses are expected to be a continued drag on Ford Motor Credit Co's earnings during 1997. The finance subsidiary reported its fourth quarter profit fell 15.4 percent from a year ago to $385 million because of credit losses that matched industry trends.
"I think we should expect credit losses, as we're seeing in the whole economy, to continue to be a drag on earnings," he said, adding that Ford Credit "expects to improve their profits despite that."
Devine said credit losses were not a major concern for industry sales, saying rates for losses and delinquent car loans are well below their recent peaks in 1989 and 1990.
